prompt: Why do I need a Kilopower reactor at all?
answer:
Reactors supply power at the Mars base. The app balances energy each sol, using reactors first, then solar, then the battery. The cargo phase needs 26.355 kW, and four reactors give 35 kW [S8]. Each reactor delivers 8.75 kW [S5].

The notes say the cargo phase rules out three reactors with no solar (Rucker et al. 2016, Table 3), so reactors are the power source that doesn't depend on sunlight. Each reactor is also heavy, at 1,754 kg [S5], and the four reactors count against lander A's limit of 18,430 kg [S3].

The source notes split that into 19.7 kW for the oxygen plants and 6.655 kW for cooling the return rocket (Rucker et al. 2016, Table 3). The notes also say this phase blocks 3 reactors with no solar. For power, the cargo phase needs 26.355 kW, and four reactors give 35 kW [S8]. Each reactor is listed at 8.75 kW delivered [S5]. The notes say 3 reactors with no solar are blocked for this phase (Rucker et al. 2016), so the reactor count is what keeps this plan at GO.

The oxygen plant (ISRU, 1,678 kg [S6]) makes oxygen from local resources. The study puts it at about 2.2 kg per hour of liquid oxygen (Rucker et al. 2016).

The screen shows the packing verdict as GO [S9] alongside these figures. Lander A's load is 17,950 of 18,430 kg [S3].

prompt: What is C3?
answer:
C3 is the departure energy for the trip from Earth to Mars, shown here as 17.6 km²/s² [S3]. In the mission, it sets how much energy the departure burn must supply to leave Earth's orbit on this route. The app's notes say that burn starts from a 407 km circular orbit around Earth (DRA 5.0, Drake 2009).

The same journey step lists the leave and arrive dates, 2035-04-18 and 2035-11-03, for a 199-day flight [S2].

prompt: Why does the trip take 199 days?
answer:
The trip takes 199 days because that is the length of the transfer for the April 18, 2035 launch date [S2]. The app finds each transfer by solving Lambert's problem, which uses the positions of Earth and Mars on that date [S5]. Those positions change with the launch date, so each departure day gives a different trip length.

Trip length is linked to departure energy. The app's crew routes show that shorter trips need more energy: the minimum-energy route took 178 days at C3 8.4, while a 120-day route needed C3 15.3 (Story mode, journey step). This launch's departure energy is C3 17.6 km²/s² [S3].

prompt: Why does suit oxygen matter more than distance?
answer:
Suit oxygen is the supply the crew breathes outside, so it sets how long the walk can safely last. The app's data shows 38% oxygen left at return [S3]. The notes say a full suit lasts 8 hours (Coan, EVA-EXP-0075), and oxygen use rises with work rate: walking is modelled at 1200 BTU/hr and working at 1050 BTU/hr (Bellcomm B70-10028). Those are the rates the model uses, not measured values from this walk.

Distance affects oxygen only through the time and effort it takes to cover it. The walk is 2,400 m and 155 min with stops [S2]. The notes also say a 20% pad is kept for emergency walkback and is applied to walking time.

The wrist warning for oxygen is set at 40%, a team choice in the app's walk rules, so the 38% left at return sits under that warning line. The walk's verdict is GO [S5].

answer:
Not for individual boulders. The terrain on this map is the Jezero site model from the USGS Mars 2020 CTX DEM at 20 m per pixel [S4]. Each height value covers a 20 m square, so a boulder much smaller than that gets averaged into its surroundings and won't show as a separate object. The model is good for broad relief, such as the slope of the ground, which is what the route figures use.

Finer detail exists elsewhere. The Jezero 1 m HiRISE DTM (USGS Mars 2020 TRN) is used for close-up 3D ground, and the notes say that view is for looking only and that route planning keeps the coarser site grids. Whether a particular boulder is visible in the 1 m data isn't something the app's data on this screen says.

prompt: How is the journey calculated?
answer:
The journey is calculated, not typed in. The app takes Earth's and Mars's positions on the leave and arrival dates from JPL's approximate planet tables (Standish), then solves a Lambert problem, which finds the transfer orbit linking those two positions (Curtis, Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students). The 199-day trip [S2] is that transfer's flight time for the 2035 window.

The departure energy, C3 of 17.6 km²/s² [S3], measures how much energy the ship needs to leave Earth orbit. The departure burn is figured from a 407 km circular orbit, as DRA 5.0 specifies.

The cruise dose of 365 mSv [S4] reflects the transit radiation rate of 1.8 mSv/day (Zeitlin et al. 2013, MSL RAD cruise data) during the flight.

prompt: Why does the crew get radiation on the way?
answer: The crew gets radiation because the ship spends the whole flight outside Earth's atmosphere and magnetic field, where cosmic rays and solar particles reach them. The app's transit figure is 1.8 mSv per day, measured on the cruise to Mars by the MSL RAD instrument (Zeitlin et al. 2013). For this journey, the cruise dose shown is 365 mSv [S4], over a flight of 199 days [S2]. The notes say faster transfers and solar-maximum timing keep crews under NASA's 600 mSv limit (Zhang et al. 2026), so the route and timing affect how much dose the crew receives.

prompt: What does the darkest sol mean?
answer: The darkest sol is the day in the Mars year with the least sunlight at this site. On that day, solar gives 0.52 kWh per m² of panel [S3]. The app balances energy once per sol over a Mars year, and the worst 420-day window decides the result (Rucker et al. 2016; ATLAS cargo-phase model). The sunlight model uses a dust optical depth of 1.0 at every site (Rucker et al. 2016), and dust dims sunlight, so dusty conditions make the darkest days darker.

Dimmed greenhouse lights grow proportionally less food (team assumption), so light output sets how much crop the beds can yield.

prompt: When do dust storms happen on Mars?
answer:
Mars dust storms cluster in a season that runs from Ls 160° to Ls 340°, centred on perihelion in late southern spring (Shirley & Mischna, NASA JPL, AGU Fall Meeting 2015). Ls is the solar longitude that marks the Mars year, so these numbers give the season's timing rather than a calendar date.

In this mission, the storm is modelled on the 2018 global dust storm at Gale. Its campaign ran from Ls 188° to Ls 248° (Guzewich et al. 2019, GRL), and the team's model has the storm reach the base at Ls 188°.

prompt: How long does the storm last?
answer:
In the app, the storm lasts about 100 sols. The app's storm model uses that length, and the source notes say the storm lasts 100 sols from its real arrival sol. The 100-sol figure matches the observed campaign in Guzewich et al. 2019, which ran about 100 sols (Ls 188° to 248°) at Gale.

The dust does not stay at its peak for that whole time. Guzewich et al. 2019 describe an exponential decay with a time scale of 43 ± 2 sols, so the haze thins steadily over the campaign. Your screen shows the peak dust opacity as tau 4.5 [S4].

The battery model drains about 0.43 kWh per km while driving. That figure is derived from Chappell, Hoffman & Bekdash 2022 and is rough. The 30% reserve is a team assumption applied as a battery reserve, and driving happens only in the first hours of each sol.

prompt: What is the IAU Mars 2000 coordinate system?
answer: The IAU Mars 2000 frame is the coordinate system the app uses for every position, because Mars has no GPS. It measures latitude as planetocentric latitude and longitude as east-positive, stored from -180 to 180 and displayed as 0 to 360 °E. Heights are relative to the Mars datum, modelled as a sphere with radius 3,396,190 m (USGS products, Gale and Jezero terrain). Rover positions in this frame come from orbital image matching and radio tracking, not satellite navigation. The view centre shown here, 18.44° N, 77.45° E [S3], is given in this frame, and its elevation of −2,570 m [S4] comes from the Jezero CTX terrain model.

prompt: What is the burn of 2.15 km/s?
answer: The 2.15 km/s burn [S3] is the departure burn: the engine firing that sends the return ship out of Mars orbit toward Earth. The app's notes say it starts from a parking orbit of 250 × 33,793 km (DRA 5.0) around Mars, whose gravity constant is 42,828.37 km³/s² (NASA Mars Fact Sheet). The departure energy, C3, is 22.4 km²/s² [S3], and it describes the same leaving trip. The burn is one of the two numbers the step shows for leaving Mars.

prompt: Where does this terrain data come from?
answer:
The elevation at the view centre, −2,570 m [S4], comes from the USGS Mars 2020 Science Investigation CTX DEM Mosaic, which gives the Jezero site terrain at 20 m/px. Inside the site's bounds, that model is used for the terrain. Everywhere else on Mars, the terrain comes from the MGS MOLA MEGDR global relief dataset from NASA's PDS Geosciences Node.

Closer to the landing site, a finer patch comes from the USGS Mars 2020 Terrain Relative Navigation HiRISE DTM mosaic, at 1 m, covering 2 x 2 km around the Octavia E. Butler landing site. This patch is used for walking on foot. Its heights are averaged to 2 m posts before use.

prompt: What can I do in this app?
answer:
This app is a Mars survival game built on NASA data. On the Martian Map you can look at the terrain of the landing sites and the wider planet, and the map shows positions in the Mars 2000 coordinate frame. You can also explore on foot at Jezero and Gale, where the game models sunlight, dust, wind, temperature and dust devils, and the walker's movement follows Mars gravity. Close-up ground in the 3D view draws fine terrain from high-resolution data where it's available.

I can explain what each part of the mission is for, why a result came out as it did, and where a number comes from. Ask me about any step or component on screen.

prompt: Where do the 3D views of the ground come from?
answer:
The close-up ground in the 3D view is 1 m terrain built from the same orbital elevation models as the site terrain. For Jezero it comes from the USGS Mars 2020 TRN HiRISE DTM mosaic, for Gale from the USGS MSL Gale Merged DEM Mosaic v3, and for Columbia Hills, Viking 2, Pathfinder and Ius Chasma from HiRISE stereo DTMs. The data is cut into tiles that load as the camera comes close.

This fine terrain is for viewing only. Route planning, slope and hazard layers use the 5-32 m site grids. The fine terrain is about 1 GB, so it isn't in the repo. It is served from the team laptop, and when the laptop is off, the app draws the site grids instead. Outside the site boxes, the rest of the planet's relief comes from MGS MOLA MEGDR (NASA PDS Geosciences Node).
